title: Flip Binary Tree To Match Preorder Traversal
statement:
`root` is a binary tree with `n` nodes whose values are the numbers `1` to `n`, each appearing once, and `voyage` is an array holding the same `n` numbers in some order. Flipping a node exchanges its left and right subtrees.

Choose the fewest nodes to flip so that the tree's preorder traversal (the node first, then its whole left subtree, then its whole right subtree) reads exactly `voyage`. Return the values of the nodes you flip, in any order. If no set of flips can produce `voyage`, return `[-1]`.
constraints: 1 <= n <= 100, where n is the number of nodes
The values in voyage are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

A preorder walk always writes the current node first and then the first value of whichever child it visits next. So while walking the tree alongside `voyage`, every node is told by the very next value of `voyage` which child must come first. If the left child is not that value, the only hope is to flip the node so the right child goes first. Nothing is a real choice, which makes this greedy walk give the smallest set of flips: a flip is made only when it is forced, and a node with a single child is never flipped because that would not change the order. Trying every set of flips would be correct but exponential.

## Approach

1. Keep `flipped` for the answer and `index` for the next unread position of `voyage`.
2. `dfs(node)` reports whether the subtree at `node` can produce the next part of `voyage`. An empty subtree always can.
3. If `node.val` differs from `voyage[index]`, it is impossible: return false.
4. Otherwise consume that value with `index++`.
5. If a left child exists but is not `voyage[index]`, record a flip of `node` and visit the right subtree before the left one.
6. Otherwise visit left, then right.
7. Return `flipped` if the whole walk succeeded, else `[-1]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`root = [1,2]`, `voyage = [2,1]`. `dfs` starts at the root with `index = 0`: `node.val` is 1 but `voyage[0]` is 2, so it returns false at once, and the answer is `[-1]`. (In Example 2, the root 1 matches, the left child 2 differs from `voyage[1] = 3`, so 1 is flipped, 3 then 2 are matched, and the answer is `[1]`.)

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each node is visited at most once.
- Space: O(n) for the recursion on a chain-shaped tree and for `flipped`.

## Pitfalls

- When the walk fails, return `[-1]`, not the flips recorded so far.
- Compare the left child with `voyage[index]` after advancing `index`, not before.
- A node with only a right child needs no flip even if the right child comes next.
- A single missing child plus a mismatch still fails; flipping cannot invent a node.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `flipped` | values of the nodes flipped so far |
| `index` | position of the next value of `voyage` to match |
| `dfs(node)` | whether `node`'s subtree can match the upcoming part of `voyage` |
| `node` | the tree node being visited |

narration.2: Collect the values of the nodes we are forced to flip.
narration.3: index points at the next value of voyage that the walk must produce.
narration.5: dfs reports whether this subtree can produce the upcoming part of voyage.
narration.6: An empty subtree adds nothing, so it always matches.
narration.9: Preorder writes this node now, so it must equal the next voyage value.
narration.10: It does not, and no flip above or below can change that: give up.
narration.12: This node is matched; move on to the next voyage value.
narration.13: The next value must start a child's subtree; if the left child is not it, the only hope is a flip.
narration.14: Record the forced flip of this node.
narration.15: After flipping, walk the right subtree first, then the left.
narration.17: No flip needed: walk left, then right, as usual.
narration.20: If the whole walk matched, return the flips; otherwise the voyage is unreachable.
